entries.content: Lu = L - Lp. Unproductive employment is the residual of total employment minus productive employment. Unproductive sectors include trade (all), FIRE (mostly), services, and government. Lu has grown secularly both in absolute terms and as a share of total employment.
Derived from total employment (L, from BLS) minus S515 (Lp). Book period from Table E.3 (chunk_30). Extension follows directly from S515 extension: Lu = L_total - Lp_extended.

Fig 5.2 shows Lu rising over time as the economy shifts toward services and finance. Fig 5.7 shows the employment composition with Lu's growing dominance, illustrating the structural transformation of US employment.

Unproductive labor does not create new value but performs necessary functions for value realization, distribution, and social reproduction. The growth of Lu is theoretically significant because these workers are paid out of surplus value, increasing the burden on productive workers.

Mohun (2013) further decomposes unproductive labor into Luw (unproductive wage workers) and Lum (unproductive management/supervisory). This decomposition reveals that within Lu, managerial employment has grown disproportionately. See mohun_employment*.csv and mohun_unproductive_decomposition*.csv.

Industry productive/unproductive assignments per Appendix B (chunk_27): Trade fully unproductive; FIRE decomposed with real estate entirely unproductive; government wages classified as unproductive unless in government enterprises. The 64-industry SIC classification in Appendix B is the definitive reference.

As a residual series, Lu inherits all measurement issues from S515. Any overcount in Lp leads to undercount in Lu and vice versa. The classification of entire sectors as unproductive (especially all of trade) is the most debated aspect of ST's methodology.
Lu = L - Lp = total unproductive labor
entries.context: Verbatim formula from Section 5.3 'Methodology: Total Labor and Productive Labor' calculation block. Direct definitional anchor for S516 construction: Lu is the residual of total employment minus productive employment.

entries.content: Productive labor is the production labor employed in capitalist production sectors: agriculture, mining, construction, transportation and public utilities, manufacturing, and productive services (defined as all services except business services, legal services, and private households, as in Table E.1).
entries.context: Verbatim definition of Lp boundary, which by complement defines the unproductive labor universe Lu = L - Lp. Establishes the sectoral scope: everything outside this list (plus nonproduction workers within these sectors) is Lu.

entries.content: Figures 5.10 and 5.11 make quite explicit that the unit wages of productive and unproductive workers change only slightly, whereas their relative employments change drastically. We can therefore unambiguously conclude that the relative decline in productive to total wages Wp/W (= V*/W) is almost entirely due to the relative decline in productive to total employment Lp/L.
entries.source_ref: ST_1994, p. 113, Section 5.3 empirical results summary
entries.context: Verbatim conclusion from Section 5.3 — the empirical centerpiece justifying ST's focus on the Lu/Lp employment composition. Confirms that Lu's rise is the structural driver, not wage differentials. Anchors Figure 5.7 / Figure 5.11 interpretation.

methodology_summary: Unproductive employment Lu = L - Lp. Residual series derived from S515. Shows secular growth reflecting shift to services, FIRE, and government. Mohun provides Luw/Lum decomposition. Industry classifications per Appendix B (chunk_27).
known_issues: Residual series — inherits all S515 measurement issues
Trade classified entirely as unproductive — debatable
Mohun's Luw/Lum decomposition reveals heterogeneity within Lu
